reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: The trial measured changes in CD8+ TILs and PD-L1 expression as biomarkers. While specific quantitative results aren't provided, the fact that these immune activation markers were measured and reported suggests some level of target engagement occurred. TLR9 agonism would be expected to activate innate immunity and increase immune cell infiltration. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: The biomarker data indicates that the intended immune activation pathway was engaged to some degree, as evidenced by changes in CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. This suggests the TLR9 agonism mechanism did modulate downstream immune biology. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: Despite evidence of biological activity, clinical endpoints failed dramatically. ORR was only 7.4% overall (7.7% monotherapy, 7.1% combination), which is well below any meaningful response threshold for melanoma. PFS was also poor at ~2 months in both arms. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: No subgroup analyses were reported, so we cannot identify any responding subsets. 5. CONFOUNDERS: The trial had a small sample size (N=27) and high rates of serious adverse events including infections (pneumonia 9.1%, sepsis 9.1%, urosepsis 16.7%) which may have limited dosing or duration. However, the treatment duration was substantial at 104 weeks, suggesting the primary issue was not timeframe.
